Context Processing: Compiler and Runtime, One Machine

Ben Um • April 18, 2026

The substrate-as-executable framing invites a natural follow-up question. If prefill is compilation and decode is execution, what performs the compilation, and what performs the execution? In traditional software architectures, these would be separate subsystems with separate designs, separate optimization concerns, and separate vocabularies. In transformer inference, they are not separate at all. The same machinery performs both roles. This chapter examines what it means for compilation and execution to share a mechanism, and why this architectural property is what makes everything else in the system possible.

Before developing the architectural argument, two terms the rest of this sub-series will lean on deserve a precise introduction. Both carry meanings from software engineering that seasoned programmers will recognize immediately. Both also have everyday counterparts that make them accessible to readers without a programming background. Establishing what each term will mean in the context of transformer inference lets the rest of the sub-series use the vocabulary freely without stopping to explain it at every turn.

A Note on the Term "Compilation"

This sub-series uses the word compilation in a specific sense that spans both everyday experience and software engineering. At the level of precision the discussion requires, compilation is the transformation of source material into a structured artifact optimized for consumption by a specific execution environment.

A chef compiles ingredients into a finished dish. The raw ingredients are source material in a form convenient for storage and acquisition. The finished dish is a transformed artifact in a form convenient for consumption by the diner. A publisher compiles a manuscript into a printed book. The manuscript is source material in a form convenient for the author's creative work. The printed book is a transformed artifact in a form convenient for the reader. A software compiler compiles source code into an executable binary. The source code is in a form convenient for the programmer to read and write. The executable is in a form convenient for the processor to run.

In every case, compilation is source-to-artifact transformation. The input is prepared material in one form. The output is the same material transformed into a different form that serves a specific downstream use. The transformation is not reversible in general — you cannot recover the original manuscript from the printed book with perfect fidelity, and you cannot recover the original source code from the executable without substantial work.

The prefill phase described in earlier chapters of the Inference Series fits this definition exactly. The composed prompt is source material. The KV substrate is the transformed artifact. The transformation is optimized for consumption by the attention mechanism that will consult the substrate during generation. When this sub-series refers to prefill as compilation, it is using compilation in this general source-to-artifact sense — not in any narrower sense specific to traditional software development.

A Note on the Term "Preprocessing"

The work of assembling a composed prompt before it reaches the model also has a name that seasoned programmers will recognize. For decades, software engineers have used preprocessing to reshape source code before it reaches the compiler — expanding macros, including header files, applying conditional compilation, rendering templates, and generally preparing the final source material that will actually be compiled. Preprocessing is not compilation itself. It is the stage upstream of compilation, where source material gets assembled into the form the compiler will transform.

The everyday counterpart is universal. Before cooking, a chef does prep work — gathering ingredients, washing vegetables, measuring portions, organizing the workspace. Before a presentation, a speaker prepares slides, organizes notes, and arranges the room. Before any substantial work begins, there is preparation that gets source material into the form the main work will act on. This preparation is structurally distinct from the main work itself.

The same structural stage exists in LLM inference. System prompts, user messages, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and prior conversation history are assembled into a composed prompt by preprocessing work that happens before any compilation begins. That composed prompt is then handed to the model, which compiles it into the substrate and executes against that substrate to produce output. The work of designing what the composed prompt will look like — system prompt design, template rendering, retrieval configuration, context composition — is preprocessing in exactly the sense seasoned programmers have been practicing for decades. The specific techniques are different, but the structural role is the same: preprocessing prepares source material; the model processes it.

With these two terms established, the architectural argument can proceed. The rest of this chapter examines what it means for compilation and execution to share a single mechanism, and why that shared machinery is what makes transformer inference a genuinely new kind of computational unit.

The Collapse

In normal software, a compiler produces artifacts that a separate runtime executes. The two subsystems are distinct, with different performance profiles and different design concerns. Transformer inference does not preserve this separation. The same machinery does both.

The same transformer layers that compile the prompt during prefill also consult the substrate during decode. The same weight matrices that produce K and V vectors at each layer during prefill also produce Queries that read from those vectors during decode. Prefill and decode are not two different mechanisms. They are the same mechanism operating in two different modes, distinguished only by what the surrounding system does with the outputs of each forward pass.

In prefill mode, the forward pass runs over the full token sequence in parallel. The K and V vectors computed at each position are retained in the substrate. No tokens are generated during prefill — prediction hasn't started yet. Prefill's job is purely constructive: it compiles the composed prompt into the substrate that decode will later consult. The output that matters is the compiled substrate.

Between prefill and decode sits a single handoff step. At the final position of the prompt — the last token in the composed input — the forward pass produces a hidden state that summarizes everything the substrate has compiled so far. That hidden state is scored against every possible next token in the model's vocabulary, producing a probability distribution over candidates. The first generated token is selected from that distribution and becomes the first token of decode. This is the moment prediction begins. Prefill built the substrate; the final prefill hidden state produced the first token of the decode phase; decode takes over from there.

In decode mode, the forward pass runs on one token at a time. The K and V vectors for the new token are appended to the existing substrate. From the hidden state at that position, the model produces a probability distribution over possible next tokens, and the next token is sampled. The loop repeats for every subsequent token. The output that matters is the generated stream of tokens.

Same machinery. Different mode. Different artifact retained from each forward pass.

This means the transformer is simultaneously a compiler and a runtime for its own output format. The artifact that prefill produces is the artifact that decode consults. The K and V vectors compiled in one mode are the K and V vectors executed against in the other. There is no translation between compilation and execution. The compiler's output is directly the runtime's input, without transformation, because they are the same machinery producing and consulting the same substrate.

The CxPU

The unit of computation that performs this dual role deserves a name. In hardware taxonomy, computational units specialized for particular domains are named for the domain they serve: GPU for graphics, TPU for tensor operations, NPU for neural network workloads. The attention mechanism at the heart of transformer inference is specialized for a specific domain as well: the processing of compiled context. The natural name for this unit is the Context Processing Unit, or CxPU.

The CxPU is the machinery that performs both prefill and decode. It is the compiler, operating on source tokens to produce compiled substrates. It is the runtime, consulting compiled substrates to produce generated tokens. It is not two units that happen to be adjacent. It is one unit that plays two roles, with the role determined by how the surrounding system consumes its outputs.

Naming the CxPU explicitly is useful because it separates the conceptual unit from specific implementations. A CxPU can be instantiated on a GPU, on a TPU, on specialized inference hardware, or on general-purpose CPUs. The specific hardware running the computation is an implementation choice. The CxPU is the logical unit of context processing, regardless of what physical hardware happens to be performing it. The framework the series has been developing operates at the CxPU level, which means the reasoning carries across hardware implementations without modification.

The CxPU also gives a clean handle for talking about what happens at every layer of the fractal that will emerge as the series develops. Each scale of operation — from a single forward pass to a multi-agent swarm — involves CxPUs performing dual-role work on substrates. The vocabulary stays consistent across scales, because the unit being discussed is consistent across scales.

Why This Matters

Every architecture built on LLM inference leverages context processing. Whether the application is a chat interface, a retrieval system, an agent, a tool-calling workflow, or a multi-agent orchestration, the underlying operation is the same: human language enters the CxPU, context gets compiled into the substrate, and human-readable output is produced. The CxPU is the context processing unit at work in every one of these architectures.

This is what makes the CxPU worth naming as a distinct computational unit. It is not just the heart of a single model running inference — it is the reusable primitive that every LLM-based application is built on. A chat interface routes user input through a CxPU and returns the output. A retrieval system assembles retrieved content into input for a CxPU. A tool-calling agent invokes a CxPU, interprets its output, runs tools, and feeds the results back into another CxPU call. A multi-agent orchestration system uses a CxPU to delegate and coordinate missions across specialized sub-agents, each of which is itself a CxPU performing its own context processing work. Each architecture is a different way of arranging CxPUs and shaping the text that flows between them.

The rest of this series develops what this means in practice. How context gets composed for CxPU consumption. How multiple CxPUs interact across pipelines and orchestrations. How the universal input and output format — human-readable text — enables fractal composition at every scale. The CxPU is the common element across all of it. Understanding its role as the context processing unit is the foundation for understanding any architecture built on LLM inference.
